passage: I'm Santosh, Yash's roommate in the hostel. For eight months he was with a girl from his course, and I liked her. But I noticed things. She laughed at his plan to join a rural health project after graduation and said he should aim for a "proper" job abroad. He stopped talking about it. Then one night in March he came back early, sat on his bed and didn't switch on the light. They'd broken up. For two weeks he skipped the mess and slept through lectures. I dragged him to the canteen for chai. He didn't say much. In April I saw him at the notice board, reading about the rural project again. He applied. He told me, "I think I'd stopped being myself with her."

qa.q: What project did Yash apply to in April?
qa.a: He applied to the rural health project.

qa.q: What does Yash's line "I'd stopped being myself with her" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt regretful, realising he had dropped his own goals, like the rural project, to keep the relationship.

qa.q: How did Santosh help Yash during the hard weeks?
qa.a: He didn't lecture or pry, but kept him connected by dragging him out for chai, which gave Yash quiet company while he recovered.

qa.q: How might Yash's ex-girlfriend see the breakup?
qa.a: She may see it differently, perhaps feeling they wanted different lives, and be sad too, though the passage only shows Yash's side.

grounding: A roommate observes a young man recover from a breakup and realise his partner did not share his values.

passage:
Before: Neelam had liked Jaya from her college drama club for months. On a Monday, after rehearsal, she finally said it. Jaya smiled kindly and said, "I really like you as a friend, but not that way." Neelam laughed it off, then cried in the auto home.

During: For the next two weeks she avoided the club. She re-read old messages and felt stupid. On Saturday her cousin took her for a long walk and asked what she actually wanted in a partner. Neelam listed things: kindness, humour, someone who likes quiet evenings. "Jaya was all that," she said. "Then you know what to look for," her cousin said.

After: A month later, Neelam went back to drama. She and Jaya shared a scene. It stung a little, but less.

qa.q: What did Jaya say when Neelam told her how she felt?
qa.a: She said she really liked Neelam as a friend, but not that way.

qa.q: Why did Neelam re-read old messages and feel stupid?
qa.a: She was hurt by the rejection and embarrassed, wondering if she had misread Jaya's friendliness.

qa.q: How did the walk with her cousin help Neelam?
qa.a: Listing what she wanted in a partner turned the rejection into clarity about her own values, so it felt less like a personal failure.

qa.q: What is it like for Jaya to share a scene with Neelam afterwards?
qa.a: She may feel a bit awkward but relieved that Neelam returned, since she clearly cared about her as a friend.

grounding: It shows a young woman handling romantic rejection over several weeks and clarifying what she values in a partner.

passage: Sit, Sabina. You asked me how I knew your Phuphi's husband was the right one? Let me tell you about my friend Amandeep, before I tell you about me. She was engaged at twenty-one to a charming boy. Everyone loved him. But she noticed he never asked about her work at the library, and when she mentioned wanting to study further, he said, "After marriage you won't need to." It sat in her like a stone. She called off the engagement. Oh, the talk in the family! She cried for months. But three years later she met someone who helped her fill out her master's application. They're still married, still arguing about books. Charm is nice, beta. But look at what they want your life to be.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep work?
qa.a: She worked at the library.

qa.q: What does "It sat in her like a stone" suggest about Amandeep's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests his words left a heavy, lasting worry that his vision of her future clashed with what she valued.

qa.q: What advice does the elder give Sabina, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To look past charm and notice what a partner wants her life to be, because shared values matter more over time.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's family have seen her calling off the engagement?
qa.a: Many may have been shocked or disapproving at the time, but later they might understand why she did it.

grounding: An elder tells a young woman how a friend chose a partner based on values after ending an engagement.

passage: Four days after the breakup, Jatin had an internal exam and a hostel room he shared with Ramesh, who liked music at night. There was no quiet corner to fall apart in. On the first night Jatin kept scrolling through old photos until Ramesh gently took the phone and set it face down. 'Revise one chapter, then you can be sad for ten minutes. Deal?' Jatin laughed despite himself. He muted her chats instead of deleting them; he could decide about that later. Then he wrote down, honestly, what had not worked: she wanted to move abroad, he wanted to stay near his parents, and neither of them was wrong. The exam went average. That evening he called his sister, ate a proper dinner, and slept before midnight for the first time that week.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do when Jatin kept scrolling through old photos?
qa.a: Ramesh gently took the phone, set it face down and offered a deal: revise one chapter, then be sad for ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Jatin mute her chats instead of deleting them?
qa.a: He was still hurting and not ready to make a final decision, so muting gave him distance without forcing a choice he might regret.

qa.q: What helped Jatin get through that week despite the exam pressure?
qa.a: Small structure did: short study blocks, naming honestly why they did not fit, eating, sleeping and calling his sister. He could keep leaning on people instead of old photos.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see Ramesh's part in that week?
qa.a: Ramesh probably knew the heartbreak could not be fixed, but a light joke and a bit of structure could keep Jatin steady 🙂

grounding: Shows recovering from a breakup under exam pressure by understanding the value mismatch and rebuilding routines with a friend's help.

passage: Arnab was funny, and on their third coffee at the café near Gariahat, Gopika laughed more than she had in weeks. Then the waiter brought the wrong order, and Arnab snapped his fingers at him and said something sharp. Later, when she mentioned her plan to teach at a night school on weekends, he called it 'cute timepass'. On the auto ride home she made a list in her notes: kind to strangers, takes my work seriously, honest. He had one out of three. The next day she texted him that she had enjoyed talking but didn't feel they wanted the same things. He replied, 'Fair. Bit of a blow, honestly, but thanks for saying it straight.' She read it twice, a little sad, and a little proud of herself.

qa.q: Where did Gopika and Arnab have their third coffee?
qa.a: At the café near Gariahat.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling after reading Arnab's reply?
qa.a: Mixed feelings: a little sad to close something fun, and proud that she chose by what mattered to her rather than by the laughter alone.

qa.q: How did Gopika's list help her decide?
qa.a: It turned a vague uneasy feeling into clear values, kindness, respect for her work and honesty, so her choice was not based only on chemistry.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt receiving her text?
qa.a: Stung, since he admits it was a blow, but he chose to respect her honesty instead of arguing, which let both of them move on with dignity.

grounding: Illustrates choosing a partner by values and both people handling a rejection honestly.

passage:
"You told your parents about me?" Tanuja set down her chai on the rooftop ledge.
"Not yet," Madhav said. "After placements."
"That's what you said after mid-sems."
"Tanu, it's complicated. They want someone who'll move to Dubai with me. Settle. You know."
"And I want to do rural medicine for five years. I told you that in our first week."
"I thought you'd change your mind."
"Did you want me to?"
Madhav looked at the water tank for a long time. "Honestly? Yes."
Tanuja's eyes filled, but her voice stayed level. "Then we want different lives, Madhav. You're not a bad person. We just want different lives."
"We could try —"
"We could try for two more years and then fight about it. I'd rather be sad now than bitter later."
He nodded slowly. "Can we at least finish this chai?"
She laughed, wetly. "Yes. This chai, we can finish."

qa.q: What does Tanuja want to do for five years?
qa.a: Rural medicine.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when her eyes filled but her voice stayed level?
qa.a: Tanuja felt sad and hurt, yet clear and steady that their plans for life did not match.

qa.q: What did the couple handle wisely, and what might help each of them now?
qa.a: They named the real difference in life plans honestly instead of drifting for years; now each could lean on friends and give themselves time to grieve.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhav to admit he hoped Tanuja would change her mind?
qa.a: It is probably painful and embarrassing for Madhav, but saying it honestly lets both of them see the mismatch clearly.

grounding: A young couple talks honestly about different life values and chooses to part before resentment builds.

passage: I'm Trisha, and last winter, after Dev ended our two years with a text, I did everything wrong for a week. I reread our chats at 2 a.m. I checked who he was following. I skipped two lectures and told everyone I had a cold. My roommate Anjali didn't push. She just started leaving the door open when she went for her evening walk, and on the eighth day I went with her. We walked round the lake, barely talking. On day ten I muted Dev instead of watching him. On day fifteen I told Anjali the embarrassing part: I'd ignored how often he mocked my friends, because I was scared of being alone. Saying it aloud helped. It still hurt in March. But I began a list of what I'd actually want next time. Kindness to my people is at the top.

qa.q: How did Dev end the relationship?
qa.a: With a text.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling during the first week after the breakup?
qa.a: Trisha felt heartbroken and restless, rereading chats at night and hiding the pain behind a pretend cold.

qa.q: Which steps helped Trisha recover?
qa.a: Walking with Anjali, muting Dev instead of watching him, and admitting what had been ignored all helped Trisha heal and think about values for next time.

qa.q: How might Anjali see her part in Trisha's recovery?
qa.a: Anjali chose patience over pushing, so she probably felt relieved and quietly glad when Trisha finally joined the walk.

grounding: A young adult looks back on recovering from a breakup and clarifying what to value in a future partner.

passage: Counselling centre, session note. Kamal (second year) came in two days after asking Pooja, a classmate, to go out with him. She said no, kindly and clearly. His first thought, he said, was to "keep trying till she sees it", and some friends told him to. We talked about what a clear no means, and how pushing would take away her comfort in the classroom they share. He said, "It feels like being told I'm not enough." We separated the two things: her choice, not his worth. By the end he decided to keep greetings normal in class, unfollow her for now, and spend fest week practising with his band. He looked lighter leaving. Follow-up after exams. — K. Rao, counsellor

qa.q: How did Pooja say no?
qa.a: Kindly and clearly.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling about the rejection?
qa.a: Kamal felt hurt and inadequate, as if the no meant he was not enough.

qa.q: Why was the counsellor right to steer Kamal away from 'keep trying'?
qa.a: A clear no deserves respect; pushing would take away Pooja's comfort in class, while Kamal's plan protects both of them.

qa.q: What would change for Pooja if Kamal had followed his friends' advice?
qa.a: Pooja would likely feel uneasy and pressured in class, with her clear answer ignored instead of respected.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a student handling romantic rejection by respecting the no and caring for himself.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Three weeks since Farida ended it. Today I finally stopped checking her profile.
I've been a mess. I replayed every conversation, looking for the moment I ruined it. But when I read our old chats today, I saw something else: we fought about the same things again and again. She wanted to move abroad; I want to stay near my parents. She thought my volunteering was a waste of time. I thought her plans ignored mine.
We liked each other. But we didn't want the same life.
It still hurts. I cried in the bathroom at work. But I went for a run after, and called my cousin, and cooked a proper dinner for the first time in weeks.
Next time, I want to talk about values early, not just about films.
— Santosh

qa.q: How long has it been since Farida ended the relationship?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when reading the old chats?
qa.a: Santosh felt sad but also clearer, realising they wanted different lives.

qa.q: What healthy steps did Santosh take to recover?
qa.a: Stopping the profile checks, running, calling a cousin and cooking a proper dinner.

qa.q: How might Farida have seen the relationship?
qa.a: Farida probably also felt the pull between her plans to move abroad and Santosh's wish to stay, which may be why she ended it.

grounding: In a diary a young adult recovers from a breakup and sees the value of compatible life goals.

passage:
In the small town, Jatin's family had arranged for him to meet a girl, Sneha's cousin Radhika. On paper, everything matched: same community, good jobs.
They met at a café near the bus stand. Radhika asked, "What do you do on Sundays?" Jatin said he teaches kids at the government school. She laughed. "Why waste time on that?"
Later, Jatin told his friend Varun, "She was nice. But she laughed at the one thing I care about most."
Varun said, "Does that matter more than the job match?"
Jatin thought for a long time. "Yes."
He told his parents gently that it wasn't right. His mother sighed but said, "Better you know now."

qa.q: What does Jatin do on Sundays?
qa.a: Teaches kids at the government school.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when Radhika laughed at his teaching?
qa.a: Jatin felt hurt and disappointed that she dismissed what mattered most to him.

qa.q: What helped Jatin decide, and what could others learn from it?
qa.a: Varun's question helped Jatin see that shared values mattered more than matching on paper.

qa.q: How might Jatin's mother see his decision?
qa.a: His mother is a bit disappointed but accepts it, seeing it's better to know early.

grounding: A young man in a small town chooses to prioritise shared values over a matching profile.

passage:
Three weeks after Noa ended it, Nadia still picked up her phone every night in her Lisbon flat to text her. Noa had been kind but clear: she wanted to move to Berlin for good, and Nadia wanted to stay near her mother, who was getting older. Neither of them was wrong. That was the hardest part.
Nadia's friend Inês made her write two lists: what she loved about Noa, and what she needed in a partner. The second list surprised her. Staying near family was on it. So was someone who talked about plans, not just feelings.
She deleted the draft messages. On Sundays she started running by the river again with Inês, slow and badly.
Some nights still hurt. But she stopped reading their old chats, and one morning she realised she had gone a whole day without checking whether Noa had posted.

qa.q: Where did Noa want to move for good?
qa.a: Noa wanted to move to Berlin for good.

qa.q: What did the second list reveal to Nadia, and how did it make her feel?
qa.a: Nadia felt surprised and a little steadier, seeing that staying near family and talking about plans were real needs in a partner.

qa.q: What small steps helped Nadia recover, and why?
qa.a: Deleting the drafts, running with Inês and not reading old chats helped, because they broke the habit of reaching back and filled the time with support.

qa.q: How might Noa have felt ending a relationship where neither was wrong?
qa.a: Noa probably felt sad and torn too, but clear that staying would mean one of them giving up something important.

grounding: Shows a young adult recovering from a breakup caused by different life values and clarifying what she needs in a partner.

passage:
In the college library, between the tall shelves, Thomas finally said it. "Shalini, would you want to go out sometime? Like, on a date."
Shalini closed her book slowly. "Thomas, I really like you as a friend. But I don't feel that way. I'm sorry."
His face went hot. He had rehearsed everything except this answer. For a second he wanted to make a joke, or say he was only kidding.
Instead he nodded. "Okay. Thanks for being honest. Still friends for the stats assignment?"
She smiled, relieved. "Obviously."
That evening he went for a long walk round the campus lake and let himself feel rotten. He texted his older brother, who called back and listened. He didn't text Shalini for a few days, just to give himself space. When they met for the assignment, it was awkward for ten minutes, and then it wasn't.

qa.q: Where did Thomas ask Shalini out?
qa.a: In the college library, between the tall shelves.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when Shalini said no?
qa.a: Thomas felt embarrassed and hurt, his face going hot, and was briefly tempted to joke it away.

qa.q: What did Thomas do that helped him handle the rejection well?
qa.a: He thanked her for honesty, let himself feel sad on a walk, talked to his brother, and took a few days of space before meeting again.

qa.q: What was it like for Shalini to say no to a friend?
qa.a: Shalini probably felt nervous about hurting him and relieved when he took it kindly and kept the friendship.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult handling romantic rejection with grace and caring for himself afterwards.

passage:
Seema Didi,
You asked how I'm doing since Priti and I broke up. Better, honestly. It's been two months.
At first I kept replaying it. Everyone thought we were perfect: same college, same jokes. But every time we talked about the future, it was a fight. She wanted a big city job and a life that moved fast. I want to come back to Nashik and help run Papa's workshop, and I want time. We kept pretending that didn't matter.
You told me to write down what I actually value. I did. Family close by. Honesty about money and plans. Kindness when tired. Priti had some of that, but we wanted different lives, and that's not a small thing.
I've stopped checking her profile. I'm playing cricket again on Sundays.
Next time, I'll talk about the future on the third date, not the third year.
Santosh

qa.q: How long ago did Santosh and Priti break up?
qa.a: Two months ago.

qa.q: How does Santosh feel now about the breakup?
qa.a: Santosh feels better and clearer, though at first Santosh felt stuck replaying it.

qa.q: What would you advise Santosh before dating again?
qa.a: Keep using the values list, and talk honestly about future plans early, so compatibility is tested before years pass.

qa.q: How might Priti have experienced the fights about the future?
qa.a: Priti may have felt frustrated and unheard too, wanting a fast city life while sensing Santosh didn't share it.

grounding: Shows a young adult reflecting on a breakup over incompatible life plans and choosing partners on values next time.

passage: Leela, you asked how I'm really doing, and my roommate still calls me "Sad Sachin," so here it is. When she ended it in March, I checked her status every hour, like it would tell me something new. I replayed every fight. I was angry, then just empty. Around week three I did what you said and wrote down what we actually fought about. It was never small stuff. She wanted to move abroad right after graduation; I want to stay near my parents in Nagpur. She laughed at my weekend volunteering at the shelter. Seeing it on paper, the breakup stopped feeling like only rejection. It was also information. I muted her, went back to Sunday football, and started sleeping before two. Last week someone from my batch asked me for coffee, and I said, "Sure, but let's actually talk about what matters to us." That's new for me.

qa.q: Where does Sachin want to stay after graduation?
qa.a: Sachin wants to stay near Sachin's parents in Nagpur.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling in the first weeks after the breakup?
qa.a: Sachin felt angry and then empty, checking the ex's status every hour and replaying old fights.

qa.q: What helped Sachin move from hurt to clearer thinking?
qa.a: Writing down what they really fought about showed a clash of values, so the breakup became useful information instead of pure rejection.

qa.q: How might Leela feel hearing that the advice worked?
qa.a: Leela might feel relieved to see a friend recovering, and quietly glad the suggestion helped.

grounding: Shows a young adult recovering from a breakup and starting to choose a partner on shared values.
